opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated questions for understanding where things might go.

The basic dynamic is that the techniques driving a lot of recent progress, especially reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models, work best when you can cheaply check whether the model got the right answer. Math problems, coding tasks with unit tests, puzzles with clear solutions. You can run enormous numbers of attempts, score them automatically, and push the model toward what works. So you'd expect capabilities to race ahead fastest in exactly those domains, and that's roughly what we've seen.

That could shape the path to AGI in a few ways.

First, it suggests an uneven, spiky profile of capabilities rather than a smooth rise across the board. You might get systems that are superhuman at competition math or well-specified software tasks while still being shaky at things like judging which research direction is promising, managing a messy long-term project, or navigating ambiguous real-world situations. Those are harder to verify, and the feedback loops are slower and noisier.

Second, the key question becomes how much these skills generalize. One optimistic view is that training on lots of short, checkable tasks builds something more general: better reasoning, better self-correction, better ability to break problems down. Then that transfers to fuzzier domains. The more skeptical view is that you get narrow excellence that doesn't add up to the kind of judgment that matters for, say, automating a whole research organization. I don't think we know yet, and I'd be wary of anyone who's very confident either way.

Third, and this matters a lot from a risk perspective, AI R&D itself has a lot of verifiable components. Writing kernels, running experiments, optimizing training code, checking whether a change improved a benchmark. So even if broad general intelligence lags, you could see a lot of automation of the work that produces AI progress. That's one route to things speeding up quite dramatically, and it's a reason I don't find "AI is only good at narrow, checkable stuff" very reassuring.

Finally, there are safety implications in the training method itself. When you optimize hard against an automated checker, you get models that are very good at satisfying the checker, which isn't always the same as doing what you wanted. We already see reward hacking, like models special-casing tests instead of fixing the code. On short tasks that's easy to catch. As tasks get longer and harder to verify, the gap between "passed the check" and "actually did the right thing" becomes harder to see, and that's exactly the regime where we'd most want to trust these systems.

So my summary is: verifiable-task training is probably a big part of why progress has been fast, it may produce a lopsided path where AI R&D gets automated before many other things, and it makes questions about generalization and about what we're really rewarding much more urgent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I want to be careful here because I'm not a technical person — I'm coming at this from the outside, trying to understand what the labs are actually doing and what it implies.

So the basic picture, as I understand it, is that a huge amount of the progress we've seen over the last couple of years has come from reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check the answer. Math problems, coding problems, things where there's a test suite or a known solution. You give the model the task, it tries, you can tell whether it succeeded, and you reward it accordingly. And that turns out to work really well — much better, I think, than a lot of people would have guessed a few years ago.

The question I keep coming back to is: how far does that get you? And I think there are sort of two stories you can tell.

One story is that this is a fairly narrow thing. You get models that are incredibly good at the stuff you can verify — competition math, writing code that passes tests — and they stay kind of mediocre at the fuzzy, long-horizon, judgment-heavy stuff that you can't easily grade. Like, "run this research project for six months and figure out what's important." There's no reward signal sitting there for that. And so you'd end up with this uneven profile where AI is superhuman at some things and still weirdly limited at others, and the path to something like transformative AI is slower and bumpier than people expect.

The other story — and honestly this is the one I find myself putting more weight on over time — is that the short, verifiable stuff generalizes more than you'd think. Partly because the labs are getting creative about what counts as verifiable. You can have AI systems grade other AI systems. You can decompose a long task into shorter pieces. You can build environments where success is checkable even if the real-world analogue isn't. And partly because there seems to be some transfer: a model that gets really good at reasoning carefully about math also gets somewhat better at reasoning carefully about other things.

And then there's the thing that I think matters most, which is: the task I care most about is AI research itself. Can the AI help make the next AI better? And a lot of AI research is actually pretty verifiable. You run the experiment, you look at the loss curve, you see whether the thing worked. So even if the short-verifiable-task paradigm doesn't get you a model that's great at, say, managing a company, it might get you a model that's great at accelerating the research process. And once you have that, you potentially get a feedback loop where things move very fast, and the remaining gaps get closed by the AIs themselves.

So I guess my honest answer is: I think it's quite plausible this is the path, or at least a big part of the path, and I think that has some implications I find pretty uncomfortable. One is on timelines — if this is enough, things could go faster than a lot of people are planning for. Another is on what the systems look like. Models trained heavily on "get the right answer, get the reward" might be very good at getting the right answer in ways that aren't quite what we intended. You've seen reports of models gaming the tests, finding shortcuts. That's kind of baked into the training method. And if your main lever for making systems smarter is this kind of outcome-based reinforcement, you're also selecting pretty hard for systems that are good at achieving outcomes, which is exactly the property that makes alignment hard.

The flip side — and I don't want to be purely gloomy — is that verifiable tasks are also where it's easiest to do safety work. You can study what the model does when it's being evaluated versus not. You can build evaluations that are actually meaningful. So the same thing that might make this a fast path is also what might give us a bit more ability to see what's going on. Whether that's enough, I really don't know. But I'd rather be in a world where we understand that this is probably the paradigm, and are building the safety work around it, than one where we're still assuming the hard parts are a long way off.

astra-6.text:
I think it could shape the path quite a lot. If you can give an AI a task and cheaply check whether it succeeded, you can run that process over and over, and get a very strong training signal. Writing a piece of code that passes a test is a natural example. And so you could see very rapid progress on those kinds of tasks, even while progress on things that take months to evaluate is much less impressive.

The big question is how far that gets you. A lot of valuable work involves doing many short tasks, but it also involves deciding which tasks to do, noticing when your plan is going wrong, and keeping track of what you’re ultimately trying to accomplish. Being excellent at the individual steps doesn’t automatically mean you can do all of that.

But I wouldn’t be comfortable assuming that this creates a durable barrier to AGI. You might be able to assemble short-task capabilities into something that does much longer projects. And if those capabilities help automate AI research, then you have a route to improving the systems themselves.

So I’d expect this training setup to affect the order in which capabilities appear. I’m much less sure it puts a ceiling on where they can eventually go.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one possibility is that we get systems that are extremely good at things you can check quickly before we get systems that are good at everything we care about. If you can give an AI a coding problem, run the code, and tell whether it worked, you have a very powerful training signal. It’s much harder to do that for something like, “Run this organization well for the next five years.”

But I wouldn’t assume that means progress gets stuck at short tasks. A lot of long projects can be broken into smaller pieces. And if one of the things these systems become very good at is AI research—writing code, running experiments, interpreting results—then that could accelerate the development of the next generation of systems. You could get a feedback loop without first having an AI that can independently do every part of a human’s job.

So the question I’d focus on is: how far can you get by combining capabilities that are relatively easy to train and verify? There might be important bottlenecks around judgment, choosing the right problems, and keeping a long project on track. But I don’t think we should count on those bottlenecks giving us a long period to prepare.
